**Dame Gracie Fields** (born **Grace Stansfield**; 9 January 1898–27 September 1979) was a British actress, singer, and comedian. A star of cinema and [music hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_hall "Music hall"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-2) she was one of the top ten film stars in Britain during the 1930s and was considered the highest-paid film star in the world in 1937.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-heritage-3) Fields was known affectionately as _Our Gracie_ and _the Lancashire Lass_ and for never losing her strong, native Lancashire accent.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-4) She was appointed a [Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_British_Empire "Order of the British Empire") and an [Officer of the Venerable Order of St John (OStJ)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venerable_Order_of_Saint_John "Venerable Order of Saint John") in 1938, and a [Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire (DBE)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dame_Commander_of_the_Order_of_the_British_Empire "Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire") in 1979.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-:0-5)

## Life and work

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gracie_Fields&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Life and work")]

### Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gracie_Fields&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early life")]

Fields was born Grace Stansfield, a daughter of Frederick Stansfield (1874–1956) and his wife Sarah Jane 'Jenny' Stansfield née Bamford (1879–1953), over a [fish and chip shop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fish_and_chips "Fish and chips") owned by her grandmother, Sarah Bamford, in Molesworth Street, [Rochdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rochdale "Rochdale"), [Lancashire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancashire "Lancashire"). Her great-grandfather, William Stansfield (b.1805), of [Hebden Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebden_Bridge "Hebden Bridge"), [Yorkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire "Yorkshire"), was a descendant of the Stansfield family of [Stansfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stansfield,_West_Yorkshire "Stansfield, West Yorkshire"), [Yorkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire "Yorkshire").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-6)

Fields made her first stage appearance as a child, in 1905, joining children's repertory theatre groups such as "Haley's Garden of Girls" and Clara Coverdale's "Nine Dainty Dots".[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Her two sisters, Edith Fields and [Betty Fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betty_Fields "Betty Fields"), and brother, [Tommy Fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tommy_Fields "Tommy Fields"), all went on to appear on stage,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-7) but Gracie was the most successful. Her professional debut in variety took place at the Rochdale Hippodrome theatre in 1910, and she soon gave up her job in the local [cotton mill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotton_mill "Cotton mill"), where she was a half-timer, spending half a week in the mill and the other half at school. Early newspaper clippings show her appearing locally in venues such as [Todmorden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Todmorden "Todmorden") (December 1913),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-8)[Milnrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milnrow "Milnrow") (February 1914),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-9) and [Burnley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burnley "Burnley") (July 1914),[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-Burnley-10) with an appearance at The Palace in Blackpool in April 1914.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-11) The Burnley newspaper described her as “The Girl with the Double Voice”.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-Burnley-10)

Fields met the comedian and impresario [Archie Pitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Pitt "Archie Pitt") and they began working together in Percy Hall's touring show _Yes, I Think So_. Pitt gave Fields champagne on her 18th birthday, and wrote in an autograph book to her that he would make her a star. Pitt began to manage her career and they began a relationship; they married in 1923 at [Clapham Register Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clapham "Clapham"). Their first revue together, written by Pitt, was called _It's A Bargain!_ in 1915, and the two continued to tour Britain together until 1931.

Throughout the period 1918–1924, they appeared in the revue _Mr Tower of London_, which took Fields to the [West End](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_End_theatre "West End theatre") for the first time. Other shows following with Pitt in subsequent years were _The Show's The Thing_ and _Walk This Way_.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Pitt was the brother of Bert Aza, founder of the Aza Agency, which was responsible for many entertainers of the day, including the actor and comedian [Stanley Holloway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Holloway "Stanley Holloway"), who was introduced to Aza by Fields, and [Betty Driver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betty_Driver "Betty Driver"), who was discovered by Archie; she was a replacement cast member in _Mr Tower of London_. Fields and Holloway first worked together on her film _[Sing As We Go](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sing\_As\_We\_Go "Sing As We Go")_, in 1934 and the two remained close friends for the rest of their lives.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-12)

### Fame

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gracie_Fields&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Fame")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e1/Gracie_Fields_1937.jpg/250px-Gracie_Fields_1937.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gracie_Fields_1937.jpg)

Gracie Fields in 1937

Fields came to major public notice in _Mr Tower of London_, a show staged in [London's West End](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_End_of_London "West End of London").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-heritage-3) Her career accelerated from this point, with [dramatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drama_(art_form) "Drama (art form)") performances and the beginning of a recording career with the [His Master's Voice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/His_Master's_Voice_(British_record_label) "His Master's Voice (British record label)"). She was one of the most successful recording artists at the label: her first record, _My Blue Heaven_ sold 500,000 copies in 1928. In 1933, His Master's Voice produced the four millionth Fields record, which was pressed by the singer herself on camera and celebrated with a special 'Lancashire Lunch' at the [Trocadero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trocad%C3%A9ro,_Paris "Trocadéro, Paris").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-13)

At one point, Fields was playing three shows a night in the West End. She appeared in the production _SOS_ with [Gerald Du Maurier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Du_Maurier "Gerald Du Maurier"), a play staged at the [St James's Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_James's_Theatre "St James's Theatre").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Fields' most famous song, "[Sally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sally_(Gracie_Fields_song) "Sally (Gracie Fields song)")", which became her theme, was written for her first film, _[Sally in Our Alley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sally\_in\_Our\_Alley\_(1931\_film) "Sally in Our Alley (1931 film)")_ (1931), a major box office hit.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-encyclopedia-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-15) She went on to make a number of films, initially in Britain and later in the United States[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-:0-5) (when she was paid a record fee of £200,000 for four films). Regardless, she never enjoyed performing without a live audience, and found the process of film-making boring.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] She tried to opt out of filming, before director [Monty Banks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monty_Banks "Monty Banks") persuaded her otherwise, landing her a lucrative Hollywood deal.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Fields demanded that the four pictures be filmed in Britain and not Hollywood.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The final few lines of the song "Sally", which Fields sang at every performance from 1931 onwards, were written by her husband's mistress, Annie Lipman. Fields claimed in later life that she wanted to "Drown blasted Sally with Walter with the aspidistra on top!", a reference to two other of her well-known songs, "Walter, Walter", and "[The Biggest Aspidistra In The World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Biggest_Aspidistra_In_The_World "The Biggest Aspidistra In The World")".[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-16)

The famous opera star [Luisa Tetrazzini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luisa_Tetrazzini "Luisa Tetrazzini") heard her singing an aria and asked her to sing in [grand opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_opera "Grand opera"). Fields decided to stay "where I knew I belonged."[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-17)

### Charity work

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gracie_Fields&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Charity work")]

In the 1930s, her popularity was at its peak, and she was given many honours: she became an [Officer of the Venerable Order of St John (OStJ)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venerable_Order_of_Saint_John "Venerable Order of Saint John") for her charity work, and a [Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_British_Empire "Order of the British Empire") for her services to entertainment in the [1938 New Year Honours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1938_New_Year_Honours "1938 New Year Honours"), and was granted the [Freedom of the Borough of Rochdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_the_City "Freedom of the City") in 1937.

In 1933, she set up the Gracie Fields Children's Home and Orphanage at [Peacehaven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peacehaven "Peacehaven"), [Sussex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sussex "Sussex"), for children of those in the theatre profession who could not look after their children. She kept this until 1967, when the home was no longer needed. This was near her own home in [Telscombe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telscombe "Telscombe"), and Fields often visited, with the children all calling her 'Aunty Grace'.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-18)

She donated her house in [The Bishops Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bishops_Avenue "The Bishops Avenue"), north London – which she had not much cared for, and shared with her husband Pitt and his mistress – to an orphanage after the marriage broke down. In 1939, she became seriously ill with [cervical cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cervical_cancer "Cervical cancer"). The public sent over 250,000 goodwill messages and she retired to her villa on [Capri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capri "Capri"). After she recovered, she recorded a special 78 rpm record simply called "Gracie's Thanks", in which she thanks the public for the many cards and letters she received while in hospital.

Fields also helped [Rochdale Association Football Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rochdale_A.F.C. "Rochdale A.F.C.") in the 1930s, when they were struggling to pay fees and buy sports equipment.

### World War II

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gracie_Fields&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: World War II")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e6/Gracie_Fields%2C_accompanied_by_an_RAF_orchestra%2C_entertains_airmen_at_their_Christmas_party%2C_27._Dec._1939.jpg/250px-Gracie_Fields%2C_accompanied_by_an_RAF_orchestra%2C_entertains_airmen_at_their_Christmas_party%2C_27._Dec._1939.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gracie_Fields,_accompanied_by_an_RAF_orchestra,_entertains_airmen_at_their_Christmas_party,_27._Dec._1939.jpg)

Fields, accompanied by an [RAF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Force "Royal Air Force") orchestra, entertains airmen at their 1939 Christmas party

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/The_British_Army_in_France_1940_F4074.jpg/250px-The_British_Army_in_France_1940_F4074.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_British_Army_in_France_1940_F4074.jpg)

Fields shares a joke with troops in a village near [Valenciennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valenciennes "Valenciennes"), France, April 1940

In 1939, Fields suffered a [breakdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nervous_breakdown "Nervous breakdown") and went to [Capri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capri "Capri") to recuperate.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-19)[World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") was declared while she was recovering in Capri, and Fields – still very ill after her cancer surgery – threw herself into her work and signed up for the [Entertainments National Service Association (ENSA)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainments_National_Service_Association "Entertainments National Service Association") headed by her old film producer, [Basil Dean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basil_Dean "Basil Dean"). Fields travelled to [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France") to entertain the troops in the midst of air-raids, performing on the backs of open lorries and in war-torn areas. During the war, she also paid for all servicemen and women to travel free on public transport within the boundaries of Rochdale. Once, Fields travelled to [Chester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chester "Chester") with serviceman Harrison after he had watched her perform in France. She stayed with his family of nine as a guest in their small 2 up 2 down house.

Following her divorce from Archie Pitt, she married Italian-born film director [Monty Banks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monty_Banks "Monty Banks") in March 1940. However, because Banks remained an Italian citizen and would have been interned in the United Kingdom after Italy declared war in June 1940, she went with him to North America, possibly at the suggestion of [Winston Churchill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston_Churchill "Winston Churchill"), who told her to "Make American Dollars, not British Pounds", which she did, in aid of the [Navy League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_Society_&_Sea_Cadets "Marine Society & Sea Cadets") and the Spitfire Fund. She and Banks moved to their home in [Santa Monica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Monica "Santa Monica"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"). Fields occasionally returned to Britain, performing in factories and army camps around the country. After their initial argument, [Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_the_United_Kingdom "Parliament of the United Kingdom") offered her an official apology.

Although she continued to spend much of her time entertaining troops and otherwise supporting the war effort outside Britain, this led to a decline in her popularity at home. She performed many times for [Allied](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_II "Allies of World War II") troops, travelling as far as [New Guinea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Guinea "New Guinea"), where she received an enthusiastic response from Australian personnel.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-20) In late 1945, she toured the [South Pacific Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_islands_in_the_Pacific_Ocean "List of islands in the Pacific Ocean").

### Post-war career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gracie_Fields&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Post-war career")]

Lancashire writer and broadcaster [Thomas Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Thompson_(writer) "Thomas Thompson (writer)") made three programmes (1945, 1946, 1947) about Fields. They were friends - she, too, had been a half-timer in the mills - and he mentions their friendship in _Lancashire for Me_.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-21)

After the war, Fields continued her career less actively. She began performing in Britain again in 1948, headlining the [London Palladium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Palladium "London Palladium") over [Ella Fitzgerald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ella_Fitzgerald "Ella Fitzgerald") who was also on the bill. The [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC") gave her her own weekly radio show in 1947, dubbed _Our Gracie's Working Party_, in which 12 towns were visited by Fields. A live show of music and entertainment, it was compèred by Fields, who also performed, together with local talents. The tour commenced in Gracie's hometown of Rochdale. Like many BBC shows at the time, this show transferred to [Radio Luxembourg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_Luxembourg_(English) "Radio Luxembourg (English)") in 1950, where it was sponsored by Wisk soap powder. [Billy Ternent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Ternent "Billy Ternent") and his Orchestra accompanied her.

In 1951, Fields took part in the cabaret which closed the [Festival of Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Festival_of_Britain "Festival of Britain") celebrations.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-22) She proved popular once more[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_], though never regaining the status she enjoyed in the 1930s. She continued recording, but made no more films, moving more towards light classical music as popular tastes changed, often adopting a religious theme. She continued into the new medium of [LP records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LP_record "LP record"), and recorded new versions of her old favourite songs, as well as contemporary tracks, to 'liven things up a bit'.

Her husband, Monty Banks, died on 8 January 1950[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-tmb-banksdead-23) of a heart attack, while travelling on the [Orient Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orient_Express "Orient Express"). On 18 February 1952 in Capri, Fields married Boris Alperovici (d.1983), a Romanian radio repairman.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-yahoo-boris-24) She claimed that he was the love of her life, and that she could not wait to propose to him. She proposed on Christmas Day in front of friends and family. They married at the Church of St Stefano on Capri in a quiet ceremony, before honeymooning in [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome").

She lived on her beloved [Isle of Capri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capri "Capri") for the remainder of her life, at her home _La Canzone Del Mare_ (_The Song of the Sea_), where her home overlooked the swimming and restaurant complex. It was favoured by many Hollywood stars during the 1950s, with regular guests including [Richard Burton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Burton "Richard Burton"), [Elizabeth Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Taylor "Elizabeth Taylor"), [Greta Garbo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo "Greta Garbo") and [Noël Coward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No%C3%ABl_Coward "Noël Coward").

### Later years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gracie_Fields&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Later years")]

Fields began to work less, but still toured the UK under the management of [Harold Fielding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Fielding "Harold Fielding") (manager of top artists of the day such as [Tommy Steele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tommy_Steele "Tommy Steele") and [Max Bygraves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Bygraves "Max Bygraves")). Her UK tours proved popular, and in the mid-1960s she gave farewell tours in Australia, Canada and America; the last performance was recorded and released years later.

In 1956, Fields was the first actress to portray [Miss Marple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miss_Marple "Miss Marple") on screen,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-gwldrec-25) in a US television ([Goodyear Playhouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodyear_Television_Playhouse "Goodyear Television Playhouse")) production of [Agatha Christie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agatha_Christie "Agatha Christie")'s _[A Murder is Announced](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Murder\_is\_Announced "A Murder is Announced")_.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-26) The production featured [Jessica Tandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessica_Tandy "Jessica Tandy") and [Roger Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Moore "Roger Moore"), and predates the [Margaret Rutherford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Rutherford "Margaret Rutherford") films by five years. She also starred in Television productions of _[A Tale of Two Cities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Tale\_of\_Two\_Cities "A Tale of Two Cities")_ ([DuPont Show of the Month](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DuPont_Show_of_the_Month "DuPont Show of the Month"), 1958), _[The Old Lady Shows Her Medals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Old\_Lady\_Shows\_Her\_Medals "The Old Lady Shows Her Medals")_ ([United States Steel Hour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_United_States_Steel_Hour "The United States Steel Hour")) – for which she won a [Sylvania Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvania_Award "Sylvania Award") (1956) and received an [EMMY Award nomination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EMMY_Award "EMMY Award") for Best Single Performance by an Actress (1957) – and _[Mrs 'Arris Goes to Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mrs.\_'Arris\_Goes\_to\_Paris "Mrs. 'Arris Goes to Paris")_ ([Studio One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio_One_(American_TV_series) "Studio One (American TV series)")), which was remade years later with [Angela Lansbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angela_Lansbury "Angela Lansbury") as Mrs Harris, a charwoman in search of a fur coat (or a [Christian Dior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Dior "Christian Dior") gown in Lansbury's case).

In 1957, Fields' single "[Around the World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Around_the_World_(1956_song) "Around the World (1956 song)")" peaked at No.8 in the [UK Singles Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Singles_Chart "UK Singles Chart"), with her recording of "[Little Donkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Donkey "Little Donkey")" reaching No.20 in November 1959.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-British_Hit_Singles_&_Albums-27)

She was the subject of _[This Is Your Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/This\_Is\_Your\_Life\_(British\_TV\_series) "This Is Your Life (British TV series)")_ on 20 March 1960, when she was surprised by [Eamonn Andrews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eamonn_Andrews "Eamonn Andrews") at the [BBC Television Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shepherd's_Bush_Empire "Shepherd's Bush Empire").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-28)

Fields regularly performed in TV appearances, being the first entertainer to perform on [Val Parnell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Val_Parnell "Val Parnell")'s _[Sunday Night at the London Palladium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunday\_Night\_at\_the\_London\_Palladium "Sunday Night at the London Palladium")_.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-29) Fields had two Christmas TV specials in 1960 and 1961, singing her old favourites and new songs in front of a studio audience. 1971 saw _A Gift For Gracie_, another TV special presented by Fields and [Bruce Forsyth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Forsyth "Bruce Forsyth"). This followed on from her popularity on _[Stars on Sunday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stars\_on\_Sunday\_(TV\_series) "Stars on Sunday (TV series)")_, a religious programme on Britain's [ITV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ITV_(TV_network) "ITV (TV network)"), in which well-known performers sang hymns or read extracts from the Bible. Fields was the most requested artist on the show.

In 1968, Fields headlined a two-week Christmas stint at the [West Riding of Yorkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Riding_of_Yorkshire "West Riding of Yorkshire")'s prestigious [Batley Variety Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batley_Variety_Club "Batley Variety Club"). "I was born over a fish and chip shop – I never thought I'd be singing in one!" claimed Fields during the performance, which was recorded by the BBC.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-30)

Fields recorded an album, _Stars on Sunday_, which was released on [York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/York_Records "York Records") BYK 707 in 1971. It included the songs "Three Green Bonnets", "Forgive Me Lord", "Round the Bend of the Road", "Ave Maria" and "The Lord's Prayer".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-32) In 1975, her album _The Golden Years_ reached No. 48 in the [UK Albums Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Albums_Chart "UK Albums Chart").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-British_Hit_Singles_&_Albums-27)

In 1978, she opened the Gracie Fields Theatre, near [Oulder Hill Leadership Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oulder_Hill_Leadership_Academy "Oulder Hill Leadership Academy") in her native [Rochdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rochdale "Rochdale"), performing a concert there recorded by the BBC to open the show. Fields appeared in ten [Royal Variety Performances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Variety_Performance "Royal Variety Performance") from 1928 onwards, her last being in 1978 at the age of 80, when she appeared as a surprise guest in the finale and sang her theme song, "Sally".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-heritage-3)

Her final TV appearance came in January 1979 when she appeared in a special octogenarian edition of _[The Merv Griffin Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Merv\_Griffin\_Show "The Merv Griffin Show")_ in America, in which she sang the song she popularised in America, "[The Biggest Aspidistra in the World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Biggest_Aspidistra_in_the_World "The Biggest Aspidistra in the World")".[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-33) Fields was notified by her confidant John Taylor, while she was in America, that she had received the [Queen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_II "Elizabeth II")'s invitation to become a [Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_British_Empire "Order of the British Empire") (in the [1979 New Years Honours List](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1979_New_Year_Honours "1979 New Year Honours")), to which she replied: "Yes I'll accept, yes I can kneel– but I might need help getting back up, and yes I'll attend– as long as they don't call Boris 'Buttons'." Seven months before her death in 1979, she was invested as a [Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire (DBE)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dame_Commander_of_the_Order_of_the_British_Empire "Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire") by [Queen Elizabeth II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_II "Elizabeth II").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-:0-5)

### Death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gracie_Fields&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Death")]

Fields's health declined in July 1979, when she contracted [pneumonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pneumonia "Pneumonia") after performing an open-air concert on the [Royal Yacht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMY_Britannia "HMY Britannia"), which was docked in [Capri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capri "Capri")'s harbour.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] After a spell in hospital, she seemed to be recovering, but died on 27 September 1979, aged 81. The press reported she died holding her husband's hand, but in reality he was repairing the heating system in a different part of their Anacapri home at the time, while Gracie was in the 'Pink Apartment'[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-34) with the housekeeper, Irena.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-35) Fields was buried in Capri's Protestant Cemetery, in a white marble tomb. Her coffin was carried by staff from her restaurant.

## Honours

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gracie_Fields&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Honours")]

**Honours**

Fields was appointed [Commander of the Order of the British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commander_of_the_Order_of_the_British_Empire "Commander of the Order of the British Empire") in the [1938 New Years Honours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1938_New_Year_Honours "1938 New Year Honours"). In February 1979, she was invested as a [Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dame_Commander_of_the_Order_of_the_British_Empire "Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire")[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-London_Gazette-36) seven months before her death at her home on Capri, aged 81.

## In popular culture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gracie_Fields&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: In popular culture")]

Fields was the mystery guest on the 1 May 1955 edition of _[What's My Line?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's\_My\_Line%3F "What's My Line?")_ After [Bennett Cerf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bennett_Cerf "Bennett Cerf") asked about one of her songs, [Dorothy Kilgallen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Kilgallen "Dorothy Kilgallen") correctly guessed it was her. Fields was granted the [Freedom of Rochdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_the_City "Freedom of the City").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-37)

In early 1985, an episode of the BBC television series _Halls of Fame,_ which presented a nostalgic look at various famous regional theatres, included a medley of Fields' songs at the [Palace Theatre, Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace_Theatre,_Manchester "Palace Theatre, Manchester"), sung by [Marti Webb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marti_Webb "Marti Webb").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-38) At the 1985 [Royal Variety Performance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Variety_Performance "Royal Variety Performance"), [Su Pollard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Su_Pollard "Su Pollard") performed "Sally" in tribute to her.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-39) The following year's Performance also featured a section with a medley of Fields' songs, again sung by Webb.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-40)

Following her death, Fields was referenced in the 1987 film _[Wish You Were Here](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wish\_You\_Were\_Here\_(1987\_film) "Wish You Were Here (1987 film)")_, the 1996 film _[Intimate Relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intimate\_Relations\_(1996\_film) "Intimate Relations (1996 film)")_, and the 2006 film _[The History Boys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_History\_Boys\_(film) "The History Boys (film)")_.

_[Gracie!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie!\_(2009\_film) "Gracie! (2009 film)")_ was a 2009 biopic TV film on her life, with [Jane Horrocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Horrocks "Jane Horrocks") playing Fields and [Tom Hollander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Hollander "Tom Hollander") her husband Monty Banks. It covers Fields' career before the Second World War and the decline in her popularity during the war.

**Other honours**

Fields had two ships named after her. On 8 April 1936, Fields herself launched the [PS _Gracie Fields_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PS_Gracie_Fields "PS Gracie Fields") which was the last [paddle steamer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paddle_steamer "Paddle steamer") built for [Red Funnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Funnel "Red Funnel") as a ferry and excursion steamer. She ran on the Southampton-Cowes route until the outbreak of [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), when she was requisitioned and served as a [minesweeper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minesweeper "Minesweeper") as HMS _Gracie Fields._ She was seriously damaged by aircraft bomb during the evacuation of [Dunkirk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunkirk_evacuation "Dunkirk evacuation") and sank in 1940. In 1936, a passenger ship was also named the _Gracie Fields_.

Three oil paintings of Fields are held by [Touchstones Gallery, Rochdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Touchstones_Rochdale "Touchstones Rochdale"): in 1938, a painting by [Herbert James Gunn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_James_Gunn "Herbert James Gunn"),[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-41) in 1978, a painting by William Allan Vause,[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-42) and in 1998, a painting by Keith John Turley.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-43)

The local theatre in Rochdale, the Gracie Fields Theatre, was opened by, and named after, her in 1978.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-44)

On 3 October 2009, the final train to run on the [Oldham Loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oldham_Loop_Line "Oldham Loop Line") before it closed to be converted to a [Manchester Metrolink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_Metrolink "Manchester Metrolink") tramway, a [Class 156](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Rail_Class_156 "British Rail Class 156"), was named in her honour.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-Rochdale_Online-45)

In September 2016, a statue of Fields, created by Sean Hedges-Quinn, was unveiled outside Rochdale Town Hall, which was the first statue of a woman to be erected for over a century in [Lancashire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancashire "Lancashire").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-46)

**Dame Gracie Fields** (born **Grace Stansfield**; 9 January 1898–27 September 1979) was a British actress, singer, and comedian. A star of cinema and [music hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_hall "Music hall"),[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-2) she was one of the top ten film stars in Britain during the 1930s and was considered the highest-paid film star in the world in 1937.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-heritage-3) Fields was known affectionately as _Our Gracie_ and _the Lancashire Lass_ and for never losing her strong, native Lancashire accent.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-4) She was appointed a [Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_British_Empire "Order of the British Empire") and an [Officer of the Venerable Order of St John (OStJ)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venerable_Order_of_Saint_John "Venerable Order of Saint John") in 1938, and a [Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire (DBE)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dame_Commander_of_the_Order_of_the_British_Empire "Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire") in 1979.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-:0-5)

## Life and work

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gracie_Fields&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Life and work")]

### Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gracie_Fields&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early life")]

Fields was born Grace Stansfield, a daughter of Frederick Stansfield (1874–1956) and his wife Sarah Jane 'Jenny' Stansfield née Bamford (1879–1953), over a [fish and chip shop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fish_and_chips "Fish and chips") owned by her grandmother, Sarah Bamford, in Molesworth Street, [Rochdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rochdale "Rochdale"), [Lancashire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancashire "Lancashire"). Her great-grandfather, William Stansfield (b.1805), of [Hebden Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebden_Bridge "Hebden Bridge"), [Yorkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire "Yorkshire"), was a descendant of the Stansfield family of [Stansfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stansfield,_West_Yorkshire "Stansfield, West Yorkshire"), [Yorkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire "Yorkshire").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-6)

Fields made her first stage appearance as a child, in 1905, joining children's repertory theatre groups such as "Haley's Garden of Girls" and Clara Coverdale's "Nine Dainty Dots".[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Her two sisters, Edith Fields and [Betty Fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betty_Fields "Betty Fields"), and brother, [Tommy Fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tommy_Fields "Tommy Fields"), all went on to appear on stage,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-7) but Gracie was the most successful. Her professional debut in variety took place at the Rochdale Hippodrome theatre in 1910, and she soon gave up her job in the local [cotton mill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cotton_mill "Cotton mill"), where she was a half-timer, spending half a week in the mill and the other half at school. Early newspaper clippings show her appearing locally in venues such as [Todmorden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Todmorden "Todmorden") (December 1913),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-8)[Milnrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milnrow "Milnrow") (February 1914),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-9) and [Burnley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burnley "Burnley") (July 1914),[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-Burnley-10) with an appearance at The Palace in Blackpool in April 1914.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-11) The Burnley newspaper described her as “The Girl with the Double Voice”.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-Burnley-10)

Fields met the comedian and impresario [Archie Pitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archie_Pitt "Archie Pitt") and they began working together in Percy Hall's touring show _Yes, I Think So_. Pitt gave Fields champagne on her 18th birthday, and wrote in an autograph book to her that he would make her a star. Pitt began to manage her career and they began a relationship; they married in 1923 at [Clapham Register Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clapham "Clapham"). Their first revue together, written by Pitt, was called _It's A Bargain!_ in 1915, and the two continued to tour Britain together until 1931.

Throughout the period 1918–1924, they appeared in the revue _Mr Tower of London_, which took Fields to the [West End](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_End_theatre "West End theatre") for the first time. Other shows following with Pitt in subsequent years were _The Show's The Thing_ and _Walk This Way_.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Pitt was the brother of Bert Aza, founder of the Aza Agency, which was responsible for many entertainers of the day, including the actor and comedian [Stanley Holloway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Holloway "Stanley Holloway"), who was introduced to Aza by Fields, and [Betty Driver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betty_Driver "Betty Driver"), who was discovered by Archie; she was a replacement cast member in _Mr Tower of London_. Fields and Holloway first worked together on her film _[Sing As We Go](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sing\_As\_We\_Go "Sing As We Go")_, in 1934 and the two remained close friends for the rest of their lives.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-12)

### Fame

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gracie_Fields&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Fame")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e1/Gracie_Fields_1937.jpg/250px-Gracie_Fields_1937.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gracie_Fields_1937.jpg)

Gracie Fields in 1937

Fields came to major public notice in _Mr Tower of London_, a show staged in [London's West End](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_End_of_London "West End of London").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-heritage-3) Her career accelerated from this point, with [dramatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drama_(art_form) "Drama (art form)") performances and the beginning of a recording career with the [His Master's Voice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/His_Master's_Voice_(British_record_label) "His Master's Voice (British record label)"). She was one of the most successful recording artists at the label: her first record, _My Blue Heaven_ sold 500,000 copies in 1928. In 1933, His Master's Voice produced the four millionth Fields record, which was pressed by the singer herself on camera and celebrated with a special 'Lancashire Lunch' at the [Trocadero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trocad%C3%A9ro,_Paris "Trocadéro, Paris").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-13)

At one point, Fields was playing three shows a night in the West End. She appeared in the production _SOS_ with [Gerald Du Maurier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Du_Maurier "Gerald Du Maurier"), a play staged at the [St James's Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_James's_Theatre "St James's Theatre").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Fields' most famous song, "[Sally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sally_(Gracie_Fields_song) "Sally (Gracie Fields song)")", which became her theme, was written for her first film, _[Sally in Our Alley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sally\_in\_Our\_Alley\_(1931\_film) "Sally in Our Alley (1931 film)")_ (1931), a major box office hit.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-encyclopedia-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-15) She went on to make a number of films, initially in Britain and later in the United States[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-:0-5) (when she was paid a record fee of £200,000 for four films). Regardless, she never enjoyed performing without a live audience, and found the process of film-making boring.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] She tried to opt out of filming, before director [Monty Banks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monty_Banks "Monty Banks") persuaded her otherwise, landing her a lucrative Hollywood deal.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Fields demanded that the four pictures be filmed in Britain and not Hollywood.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The final few lines of the song "Sally", which Fields sang at every performance from 1931 onwards, were written by her husband's mistress, Annie Lipman. Fields claimed in later life that she wanted to "Drown blasted Sally with Walter with the aspidistra on top!", a reference to two other of her well-known songs, "Walter, Walter", and "[The Biggest Aspidistra In The World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Biggest_Aspidistra_In_The_World "The Biggest Aspidistra In The World")".[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-16)

The famous opera star [Luisa Tetrazzini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luisa_Tetrazzini "Luisa Tetrazzini") heard her singing an aria and asked her to sing in [grand opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_opera "Grand opera"). Fields decided to stay "where I knew I belonged."[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-17)

### Charity work

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gracie_Fields&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Charity work")]

In the 1930s, her popularity was at its peak, and she was given many honours: she became an [Officer of the Venerable Order of St John (OStJ)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venerable_Order_of_Saint_John "Venerable Order of Saint John") for her charity work, and a [Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_British_Empire "Order of the British Empire") for her services to entertainment in the [1938 New Year Honours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1938_New_Year_Honours "1938 New Year Honours"), and was granted the [Freedom of the Borough of Rochdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_the_City "Freedom of the City") in 1937.

In 1933, she set up the Gracie Fields Children's Home and Orphanage at [Peacehaven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peacehaven "Peacehaven"), [Sussex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sussex "Sussex"), for children of those in the theatre profession who could not look after their children. She kept this until 1967, when the home was no longer needed. This was near her own home in [Telscombe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telscombe "Telscombe"), and Fields often visited, with the children all calling her 'Aunty Grace'.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-18)

She donated her house in [The Bishops Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bishops_Avenue "The Bishops Avenue"), north London – which she had not much cared for, and shared with her husband Pitt and his mistress – to an orphanage after the marriage broke down. In 1939, she became seriously ill with [cervical cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cervical_cancer "Cervical cancer"). The public sent over 250,000 goodwill messages and she retired to her villa on [Capri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capri "Capri"). After she recovered, she recorded a special 78 rpm record simply called "Gracie's Thanks", in which she thanks the public for the many cards and letters she received while in hospital.

Fields also helped [Rochdale Association Football Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rochdale_A.F.C. "Rochdale A.F.C.") in the 1930s, when they were struggling to pay fees and buy sports equipment.

### World War II

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gracie_Fields&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: World War II")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e6/Gracie_Fields%2C_accompanied_by_an_RAF_orchestra%2C_entertains_airmen_at_their_Christmas_party%2C_27._Dec._1939.jpg/250px-Gracie_Fields%2C_accompanied_by_an_RAF_orchestra%2C_entertains_airmen_at_their_Christmas_party%2C_27._Dec._1939.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gracie_Fields,_accompanied_by_an_RAF_orchestra,_entertains_airmen_at_their_Christmas_party,_27._Dec._1939.jpg)

Fields, accompanied by an [RAF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Force "Royal Air Force") orchestra, entertains airmen at their 1939 Christmas party

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/The_British_Army_in_France_1940_F4074.jpg/250px-The_British_Army_in_France_1940_F4074.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_British_Army_in_France_1940_F4074.jpg)

Fields shares a joke with troops in a village near [Valenciennes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valenciennes "Valenciennes"), France, April 1940

In 1939, Fields suffered a [breakdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nervous_breakdown "Nervous breakdown") and went to [Capri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capri "Capri") to recuperate.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-19)[World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") was declared while she was recovering in Capri, and Fields – still very ill after her cancer surgery – threw herself into her work and signed up for the [Entertainments National Service Association (ENSA)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainments_National_Service_Association "Entertainments National Service Association") headed by her old film producer, [Basil Dean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basil_Dean "Basil Dean"). Fields travelled to [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France") to entertain the troops in the midst of air-raids, performing on the backs of open lorries and in war-torn areas. During the war, she also paid for all servicemen and women to travel free on public transport within the boundaries of Rochdale. Once, Fields travelled to [Chester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chester "Chester") with serviceman Harrison after he had watched her perform in France. She stayed with his family of nine as a guest in their small 2 up 2 down house.

Following her divorce from Archie Pitt, she married Italian-born film director [Monty Banks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monty_Banks "Monty Banks") in March 1940. However, because Banks remained an Italian citizen and would have been interned in the United Kingdom after Italy declared war in June 1940, she went with him to North America, possibly at the suggestion of [Winston Churchill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston_Churchill "Winston Churchill"), who told her to "Make American Dollars, not British Pounds", which she did, in aid of the [Navy League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marine_Society_&_Sea_Cadets "Marine Society & Sea Cadets") and the Spitfire Fund. She and Banks moved to their home in [Santa Monica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Monica "Santa Monica"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"). Fields occasionally returned to Britain, performing in factories and army camps around the country. After their initial argument, [Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_the_United_Kingdom "Parliament of the United Kingdom") offered her an official apology.

Although she continued to spend much of her time entertaining troops and otherwise supporting the war effort outside Britain, this led to a decline in her popularity at home. She performed many times for [Allied](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_II "Allies of World War II") troops, travelling as far as [New Guinea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Guinea "New Guinea"), where she received an enthusiastic response from Australian personnel.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-20) In late 1945, she toured the [South Pacific Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_islands_in_the_Pacific_Ocean "List of islands in the Pacific Ocean").

### Post-war career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gracie_Fields&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Post-war career")]

Lancashire writer and broadcaster [Thomas Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Thompson_(writer) "Thomas Thompson (writer)") made three programmes (1945, 1946, 1947) about Fields. They were friends - she, too, had been a half-timer in the mills - and he mentions their friendship in _Lancashire for Me_.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-21)

After the war, Fields continued her career less actively. She began performing in Britain again in 1948, headlining the [London Palladium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Palladium "London Palladium") over [Ella Fitzgerald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ella_Fitzgerald "Ella Fitzgerald") who was also on the bill. The [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC") gave her her own weekly radio show in 1947, dubbed _Our Gracie's Working Party_, in which 12 towns were visited by Fields. A live show of music and entertainment, it was compèred by Fields, who also performed, together with local talents. The tour commenced in Gracie's hometown of Rochdale. Like many BBC shows at the time, this show transferred to [Radio Luxembourg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_Luxembourg_(English) "Radio Luxembourg (English)") in 1950, where it was sponsored by Wisk soap powder. [Billy Ternent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Ternent "Billy Ternent") and his Orchestra accompanied her.

In 1951, Fields took part in the cabaret which closed the [Festival of Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Festival_of_Britain "Festival of Britain") celebrations.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-22) She proved popular once more[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_], though never regaining the status she enjoyed in the 1930s. She continued recording, but made no more films, moving more towards light classical music as popular tastes changed, often adopting a religious theme. She continued into the new medium of [LP records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LP_record "LP record"), and recorded new versions of her old favourite songs, as well as contemporary tracks, to 'liven things up a bit'.

Her husband, Monty Banks, died on 8 January 1950[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-tmb-banksdead-23) of a heart attack, while travelling on the [Orient Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orient_Express "Orient Express"). On 18 February 1952 in Capri, Fields married Boris Alperovici (d.1983), a Romanian radio repairman.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-yahoo-boris-24) She claimed that he was the love of her life, and that she could not wait to propose to him. She proposed on Christmas Day in front of friends and family. They married at the Church of St Stefano on Capri in a quiet ceremony, before honeymooning in [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome").

She lived on her beloved [Isle of Capri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capri "Capri") for the remainder of her life, at her home _La Canzone Del Mare_ (_The Song of the Sea_), where her home overlooked the swimming and restaurant complex. It was favoured by many Hollywood stars during the 1950s, with regular guests including [Richard Burton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Burton "Richard Burton"), [Elizabeth Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Taylor "Elizabeth Taylor"), [Greta Garbo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greta_Garbo "Greta Garbo") and [Noël Coward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No%C3%ABl_Coward "Noël Coward").

### Later years

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gracie_Fields&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Later years")]

Fields began to work less, but still toured the UK under the management of [Harold Fielding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Fielding "Harold Fielding") (manager of top artists of the day such as [Tommy Steele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tommy_Steele "Tommy Steele") and [Max Bygraves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Bygraves "Max Bygraves")). Her UK tours proved popular, and in the mid-1960s she gave farewell tours in Australia, Canada and America; the last performance was recorded and released years later.

In 1956, Fields was the first actress to portray [Miss Marple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miss_Marple "Miss Marple") on screen,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-gwldrec-25) in a US television ([Goodyear Playhouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodyear_Television_Playhouse "Goodyear Television Playhouse")) production of [Agatha Christie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agatha_Christie "Agatha Christie")'s _[A Murder is Announced](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Murder\_is\_Announced "A Murder is Announced")_.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-26) The production featured [Jessica Tandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessica_Tandy "Jessica Tandy") and [Roger Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roger_Moore "Roger Moore"), and predates the [Margaret Rutherford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Rutherford "Margaret Rutherford") films by five years. She also starred in Television productions of _[A Tale of Two Cities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Tale\_of\_Two\_Cities "A Tale of Two Cities")_ ([DuPont Show of the Month](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DuPont_Show_of_the_Month "DuPont Show of the Month"), 1958), _[The Old Lady Shows Her Medals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Old\_Lady\_Shows\_Her\_Medals "The Old Lady Shows Her Medals")_ ([United States Steel Hour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_United_States_Steel_Hour "The United States Steel Hour")) – for which she won a [Sylvania Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvania_Award "Sylvania Award") (1956) and received an [EMMY Award nomination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EMMY_Award "EMMY Award") for Best Single Performance by an Actress (1957) – and _[Mrs 'Arris Goes to Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mrs.\_'Arris\_Goes\_to\_Paris "Mrs. 'Arris Goes to Paris")_ ([Studio One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio_One_(American_TV_series) "Studio One (American TV series)")), which was remade years later with [Angela Lansbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angela_Lansbury "Angela Lansbury") as Mrs Harris, a charwoman in search of a fur coat (or a [Christian Dior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Dior "Christian Dior") gown in Lansbury's case).

In 1957, Fields' single "[Around the World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Around_the_World_(1956_song) "Around the World (1956 song)")" peaked at No.8 in the [UK Singles Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Singles_Chart "UK Singles Chart"), with her recording of "[Little Donkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Donkey "Little Donkey")" reaching No.20 in November 1959.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-British_Hit_Singles_&_Albums-27)

She was the subject of _[This Is Your Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/This\_Is\_Your\_Life\_(British\_TV\_series) "This Is Your Life (British TV series)")_ on 20 March 1960, when she was surprised by [Eamonn Andrews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eamonn_Andrews "Eamonn Andrews") at the [BBC Television Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shepherd's_Bush_Empire "Shepherd's Bush Empire").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-28)

Fields regularly performed in TV appearances, being the first entertainer to perform on [Val Parnell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Val_Parnell "Val Parnell")'s _[Sunday Night at the London Palladium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunday\_Night\_at\_the\_London\_Palladium "Sunday Night at the London Palladium")_.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-29) Fields had two Christmas TV specials in 1960 and 1961, singing her old favourites and new songs in front of a studio audience. 1971 saw _A Gift For Gracie_, another TV special presented by Fields and [Bruce Forsyth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Forsyth "Bruce Forsyth"). This followed on from her popularity on _[Stars on Sunday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stars\_on\_Sunday\_(TV\_series) "Stars on Sunday (TV series)")_, a religious programme on Britain's [ITV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ITV_(TV_network) "ITV (TV network)"), in which well-known performers sang hymns or read extracts from the Bible. Fields was the most requested artist on the show.

In 1968, Fields headlined a two-week Christmas stint at the [West Riding of Yorkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Riding_of_Yorkshire "West Riding of Yorkshire")'s prestigious [Batley Variety Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batley_Variety_Club "Batley Variety Club"). "I was born over a fish and chip shop – I never thought I'd be singing in one!" claimed Fields during the performance, which was recorded by the BBC.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-30)

Fields recorded an album, _Stars on Sunday_, which was released on [York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/York_Records "York Records") BYK 707 in 1971. It included the songs "Three Green Bonnets", "Forgive Me Lord", "Round the Bend of the Road", "Ave Maria" and "The Lord's Prayer".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-32) In 1975, her album _The Golden Years_ reached No. 48 in the [UK Albums Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Albums_Chart "UK Albums Chart").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-British_Hit_Singles_&_Albums-27)

In 1978, she opened the Gracie Fields Theatre, near [Oulder Hill Leadership Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oulder_Hill_Leadership_Academy "Oulder Hill Leadership Academy") in her native [Rochdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rochdale "Rochdale"), performing a concert there recorded by the BBC to open the show. Fields appeared in ten [Royal Variety Performances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Variety_Performance "Royal Variety Performance") from 1928 onwards, her last being in 1978 at the age of 80, when she appeared as a surprise guest in the finale and sang her theme song, "Sally".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-heritage-3)

Her final TV appearance came in January 1979 when she appeared in a special octogenarian edition of _[The Merv Griffin Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Merv\_Griffin\_Show "The Merv Griffin Show")_ in America, in which she sang the song she popularised in America, "[The Biggest Aspidistra in the World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Biggest_Aspidistra_in_the_World "The Biggest Aspidistra in the World")".[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-33) Fields was notified by her confidant John Taylor, while she was in America, that she had received the [Queen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_II "Elizabeth II")'s invitation to become a [Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_British_Empire "Order of the British Empire") (in the [1979 New Years Honours List](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1979_New_Year_Honours "1979 New Year Honours")), to which she replied: "Yes I'll accept, yes I can kneel– but I might need help getting back up, and yes I'll attend– as long as they don't call Boris 'Buttons'." Seven months before her death in 1979, she was invested as a [Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire (DBE)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dame_Commander_of_the_Order_of_the_British_Empire "Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire") by [Queen Elizabeth II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_II "Elizabeth II").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-:0-5)

### Death

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gracie_Fields&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Death")]

Fields's health declined in July 1979, when she contracted [pneumonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pneumonia "Pneumonia") after performing an open-air concert on the [Royal Yacht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMY_Britannia "HMY Britannia"), which was docked in [Capri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capri "Capri")'s harbour.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] After a spell in hospital, she seemed to be recovering, but died on 27 September 1979, aged 81. The press reported she died holding her husband's hand, but in reality he was repairing the heating system in a different part of their Anacapri home at the time, while Gracie was in the 'Pink Apartment'[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-34) with the housekeeper, Irena.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-35) Fields was buried in Capri's Protestant Cemetery, in a white marble tomb. Her coffin was carried by staff from her restaurant.

## Honours

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gracie_Fields&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Honours")]

**Honours**

Fields was appointed [Commander of the Order of the British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commander_of_the_Order_of_the_British_Empire "Commander of the Order of the British Empire") in the [1938 New Years Honours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1938_New_Year_Honours "1938 New Year Honours"). In February 1979, she was invested as a [Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dame_Commander_of_the_Order_of_the_British_Empire "Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire")[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-London_Gazette-36) seven months before her death at her home on Capri, aged 81.

## In popular culture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gracie_Fields&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: In popular culture")]

Fields was the mystery guest on the 1 May 1955 edition of _[What's My Line?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's\_My\_Line%3F "What's My Line?")_ After [Bennett Cerf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bennett_Cerf "Bennett Cerf") asked about one of her songs, [Dorothy Kilgallen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothy_Kilgallen "Dorothy Kilgallen") correctly guessed it was her. Fields was granted the [Freedom of Rochdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_the_City "Freedom of the City").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-37)

In early 1985, an episode of the BBC television series _Halls of Fame,_ which presented a nostalgic look at various famous regional theatres, included a medley of Fields' songs at the [Palace Theatre, Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palace_Theatre,_Manchester "Palace Theatre, Manchester"), sung by [Marti Webb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marti_Webb "Marti Webb").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-38) At the 1985 [Royal Variety Performance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Variety_Performance "Royal Variety Performance"), [Su Pollard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Su_Pollard "Su Pollard") performed "Sally" in tribute to her.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-39) The following year's Performance also featured a section with a medley of Fields' songs, again sung by Webb.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-40)

Following her death, Fields was referenced in the 1987 film _[Wish You Were Here](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wish\_You\_Were\_Here\_(1987\_film) "Wish You Were Here (1987 film)")_, the 1996 film _[Intimate Relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intimate\_Relations\_(1996\_film) "Intimate Relations (1996 film)")_, and the 2006 film _[The History Boys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_History\_Boys\_(film) "The History Boys (film)")_.

_[Gracie!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie!\_(2009\_film) "Gracie! (2009 film)")_ was a 2009 biopic TV film on her life, with [Jane Horrocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Horrocks "Jane Horrocks") playing Fields and [Tom Hollander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Hollander "Tom Hollander") her husband Monty Banks. It covers Fields' career before the Second World War and the decline in her popularity during the war.

**Other honours**

Fields had two ships named after her. On 8 April 1936, Fields herself launched the [PS _Gracie Fields_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PS_Gracie_Fields "PS Gracie Fields") which was the last [paddle steamer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paddle_steamer "Paddle steamer") built for [Red Funnel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Funnel "Red Funnel") as a ferry and excursion steamer. She ran on the Southampton-Cowes route until the outbreak of [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), when she was requisitioned and served as a [minesweeper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minesweeper "Minesweeper") as HMS _Gracie Fields._ She was seriously damaged by aircraft bomb during the evacuation of [Dunkirk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunkirk_evacuation "Dunkirk evacuation") and sank in 1940. In 1936, a passenger ship was also named the _Gracie Fields_.

Three oil paintings of Fields are held by [Touchstones Gallery, Rochdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Touchstones_Rochdale "Touchstones Rochdale"): in 1938, a painting by [Herbert James Gunn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_James_Gunn "Herbert James Gunn"),[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-41) in 1978, a painting by William Allan Vause,[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-42) and in 1998, a painting by Keith John Turley.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-43)

The local theatre in Rochdale, the Gracie Fields Theatre, was opened by, and named after, her in 1978.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-44)

On 3 October 2009, the final train to run on the [Oldham Loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oldham_Loop_Line "Oldham Loop Line") before it closed to be converted to a [Manchester Metrolink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_Metrolink "Manchester Metrolink") tramway, a [Class 156](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Rail_Class_156 "British Rail Class 156"), was named in her honour.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-Rochdale_Online-45)

In September 2016, a statue of Fields, created by Sean Hedges-Quinn, was unveiled outside Rochdale Town Hall, which was the first statue of a woman to be erected for over a century in [Lancashire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancashire "Lancashire").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gracie_Fields#cite_note-46)
